title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Classical orbital elements


When describing a satellite’s orbit, we have two common approaches:
State vectors: position \(\mathbf{r}\) and velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) at a given instant.
Classical Orbital Elements (COEs): Six geometric parameters that define the shape and orientation of the orbit.

Eccentricity (\(\mathbf{e}\))
Inclination (\(i\))
Right Ascension of the ascending node (\(\Omega\))
Argument of Perigee (\(\omega\))
True Anomaly (\(\nu\))
Semi-major axis (\(a\))

This post walks through computing COEs from state vectors in Python using NumPy.
To keep the workflow reproducible and easy to integrate, the program reads inputs and writes outputs in YAML. YAML is human-readable, machine-parseable, and widely used in configuration files, which makes it ideal for storing both raw inputs and structured outputs.
The code:

Reads the position and velocity vectors from a YAML file.
Produces outputs in three ways:

Stored in a Python dictionary (full float64 precision).
Printed on screen (rounded to 2 decimals for readability).
Written back to a YAML file (full float64 precision).

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Step 1 — Setting up the Class
class ClassicalOrbitalElements:
    """
    Computes the Classical Orbital Elements (COEs) from a position
    and velocity state vector.
    """

    def __init__(self, position, velocity, mu=MU_EARTH):
        self.r = np.array(position, dtype=float)
        self.v = np.array(velocity, dtype=float)
        self.mu = mu
        self.coe = None

        self._validate_input()
The __init__ method is the constructor of the class. It runs automatically whenever a new object is created. Line by line:
self.r = np.array(position, dtype=float) → converts the input position list into a NumPy array of floats and stores it inside the object.
self.v = np.array(velocity, dtype=float) → does the same for the velocity vector.
self.mu = mu → stores the gravitational parameter, defaulting to Earth’s \(\mu\).
self.coe = None → initializes the orbital elements; they’ll be computed later.
self._validate_input() → calls a helper method to make sure the inputs are valid before proceeding.
This ensures every object starts with clean, checked data.

Why self appears everywhere
In Python, self is a reference to the object being created. When we write:
self.r = np.array(position)
we are saving the position vector inside the object so other methods can reuse it. Each instance of ClassicalOrbitalElements carries its own memory of \(\vec{r}\), \(\vec{v}\), and computed elements.

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Step 2 - Input Validation
def _validate_input(self):
    if np.allclose(self.r, 0):
        raise ValueError("Position vector cannot be zero.")
    if np.allclose(self.v, 0):
        raise ValueError("Velocity vector cannot be zero.")
    if not np.isfinite(self.r).all() or not np.isfinite(self.v).all():
        raise ValueError("Position and velocity must contain finite numbers.")
The leading underscore (_validate_input) is a Python naming convention that signals this is an internal method. It’s not meant to be called by users of the class but rather used only inside the class itself.
np.allclose()
np.allclose(arr, 0) checks whether every element of arr is close to zero within a default tolerance (rtol=1e-05, atol=1e-08).
Examples:
np.allclose([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0)   # True
np.allclose([1e-12, 0.0, 0.0], 0) # True
np.allclose([1e-3, 0.0, 0.0], 0)  # False
This prevents “almost-zero” vectors that would make orbital elements undefined.
For more details on np.allclose() please refer to the documentation here.
np.isfinite()
This checks whether numbers are finite (not \(\infty\) or NaN).
Examples:
np.isfinite([1.0, np.inf, np.nan])
# → array([ True, False, False ])
Using .all() lets us check every element:
np.isfinite([1.0, 2.0, np.inf]).all()
# → False (because of the infinity)
This protects us against corrupted inputs like infinite velocity.

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Step 3 — Angular Momentum and Inclination
h_vec = np.cross(r, v)
h = np.linalg.norm(h_vec)
i = np.degrees(safe_arccos(h_vec[2] / h))
The specific angular momentum is:
\[
\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}.
\]
Its magnitude \(|\vec{h}|\) is constant for Keplerian motion.
Inclination \(i\) is the tilt of the orbital plane:
\[
i = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{h_z}{h}\right).
\]

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Step 4 — Node Vector and RAAN
k_hat = np.array([0, 0, 1])
n_vec = np.cross(k_hat, h_vec)
n = np.linalg.norm(n_vec)

if n != 0:
    RAAN = np.degrees(safe_arccos(n_vec[0] / n))
    if n_vec[1] < 0:
        RAAN = 360 - RAAN
else:
    RAAN = np.nan
The node vector
\[
\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{h}
\]
points to the ascending node (\(\mathbf{k} = [0, 0, 1]\)).
The Right Ascension of the Ascending Node (RAAN) is:
\[
\Omega = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{n_x}{n}\right)
\]
If \(n_y < 0\), we flip to \(360^\circ - \Omega\).
When \(i \approx 0^\circ\) (equatorial orbit), the node line is undefined. We return NaN instead of zero — because zero would falsely suggest a meaningful direction. NaN makes it explicit: RAAN is not defined in this case.

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Step 5 - Eccentricity Vector
e_vec = (1/mu) * ((v_norm**2 - mu/r_norm)*r - np.dot(r, v)*v)
e = np.linalg.norm(e_vec)
Add equation \[
\mathbf{e} = \frac{1}{\mu}
\left[ (v^2 - \tfrac{\mu}{r})\mathbf{r} - (\mathbf{r}\cdot \mathbf{v})\mathbf{v} \right]
\]
The magnitude \(e = |\vec{e}|\) defines orbit shape:

\(e=0\): circle
\(0<e<1\): ellipse
\(e=1\): parabola
\(e>1\): hyperbola

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
section: Step 6 — Argument of Perigee and True Anomaly
text:
Step 6 — Argument of Perigee and True Anomaly
if n != 0 and e > 1e-8:
    omega = np.degrees(safe_arccos(np.dot(n_vec, e_vec) / (n * e)))
    if e_vec[2] < 0:
        omega = 360 - omega
else:
    omega = np.nan
\[
\omega = \cos^{-1}\left( \frac{\mathbf{n}\cdot \mathbf{e}}{n e} \right),
\quad
\text{if } e_z < 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \omega = 2\pi - \omega
\]
But if \(e \approx 0\), the direction of perigee is meaningless → we return NaN. Again, NaN is better than zero because zero would wrongly suggest perigee lies on the x-axis.
For the true anomaly \(\nu\):
\[
\nu = \cos^{-1}\left( \frac{\mathbf{e}\cdot \mathbf{r}}{e r} \right)
\]
If \(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{v} < 0\), we take \(360^\circ - \nu\). If \(e \approx 0\), we compute \(\nu\) relative to \(\vec{n}\), unless the orbit is both circular and equatorial — in which case \(\nu\) is undefined.
For circular orbits (\(e \approx 0\)), (\(\nu\)) is measured from the node vector (\(\mathbf{n}\)).

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Step 7 — Semi-major Axis
energy = v_norm**2 / 2 - mu / r_norm
a = -mu / (2 * energy)
From specific orbital energy:
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{v^2}{2} - \frac{\mu}{r}
\]
\[
a = -\frac{\mu}{2\varepsilon}
\] If \(\epsilon \to 0\) (parabolic trajectory), \(a \to \infty\).

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Step 8 — Safe arccos with np.clip
Why do we need safe_arccos()?
Example:
x = 1.0000000002
np.arccos(x)   # ValueError
safe_arccos(x) # Works fine
By clamping values into \([-1, 1]\), np.clip ensures we never hit numerical errors even when floating-point rounding pushes us slightly out of bounds.

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
Writing output to YAML
def save_to_yaml(self, filename="coe_output.yaml"):
        if self.coe is None:
            raise RuntimeError("COEs not yet calculated. Call calculate() first.")

        with open(filename, "w") as f:
            yaml.dump(self.coe, f, default_flow_style=False)

        print(f"COEs saved to {filename}")
This method saves the computed COEs into a YAML file.

if self.coe is None: → safety check: don’t save until COEs are actually calculated.
with open(filename, "w") as f: → opens the target file in write mode.
yaml.dump(self.coe, f, default_flow_style=False) → writes the Python dictionary self.coe to the file:

self.coe: the data being written.
f: the open file handle.
default_flow_style=False: ensures YAML is written in block style (easy to read), rather than inline JSON-like style.


This produces a clean, shareable configuration-style output.

title: A Python class for computing classical orbital elements
text:
The calling program
import yaml
from core import ClassicalOrbitalElements

def main():
    # Load state vector from YAML
    with open("config.yaml", "r") as f:
        config = yaml.safe_load(f)

    position = config["state_vector"]["position"]
    velocity = config["state_vector"]["velocity"]

    coe_calc = ClassicalOrbitalElements(position, velocity)
    coe_calc.calculate()
    coe_calc.summary()
    coe_calc.save_to_yaml("orbit_output.yaml")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
This is the driver script. Its job is to:

Read the input state vectors from config.yaml.
Create a ClassicalOrbitalElements object with the data.
Compute, summarize, and save the results.

Separating this into a main.py is good practice:

Keeps the class code clean and reusable.
Lets us change how we call the class (e.g., from CLI or tests) without modifying the core logic.
Mirrors real-world software projects where library code and application entry points are distinct.

AI Attribution: A few weeks ago, I had written a function to compute COEs from a satellite’s state vector. I shared it with AI and asked to reframe it using Python classes, dictionaries, and YAML as an exercise. The AI refactored the function into a clean, class-based design with modular files, design docs, and tests. What started as a single function evolved into something much closer to industry-level code. In this post, I focused on the core class; in later posts, I’ll cover documentation and testing.

title: Automating a Scientific Python Setup: A Gentle Walkthrough
text:
Setting up scientific Python environments used to feel overwhelming to me—until I started collaborating with AI. With its help, I’ve learned how to automate my setup using shell scripts and gained confidence in managing the tools I use for orbital mechanics and data visualization.
In this post, I’ll walk you through a script that sets up a fully functional Python environment to work with Poliastro, a powerful library for orbital mechanics. Whether you’re a beginner or someone looking to streamline your workflow, this guide will give you both a working setup and an understanding of what each step does.

text:
What We’ll Do
By the end of this post, you’ll know how to:

Write and run a basic shell script
Use conda to manage environments and packages
Install the correct versions of poliastro, astropy, and other tools
Understand why versions matter in scientific computing

title: Automating a Scientific Python Setup: A Gentle Walkthrough
text:
The Full Script (Preview)
Here’s what you’ll build and understand step by step. To get started, copy the code below into a new file and save it as setup_orbitviz.sh. This script will automate the creation of your orbital mechanics Python environment.
#!/bin/bash

echo "🛰️  Creating conda environment 'orbitviz' with Python 3.10..."
conda create -y -n orbitviz python=3.10

echo "🚀 Activating environment (if this fails, activate manually)..."
conda activate orbitviz || source activate orbitviz

echo "🔭 Installing astropy 5.3..."
conda install -y -n orbitviz -c conda-forge astropy=5.3

echo "📈 Installing matplotlib 3.5..."
conda install -y -n orbitviz matplotlib=3.5

echo "🌌 Installing poliastro (with all extras)..."
conda run -n orbitviz pip install poliastro[all]

echo "📓 Installing JupyterLab..."
conda install -y -n orbitviz -c conda-forge jupyterlab

echo "🎨 Installing Plotly..."
conda install -y -n orbitviz -c plotly plotly

echo "🧮 Installing numpy, scipy, tqdm..."
conda install -y -n orbitviz numpy scipy tqdm

echo "✅ Setup complete. To activate the environment later, run: conda activate orbitviz"

title: Automating a Scientific Python Setup: A Gentle Walkthrough
text:
Line-by-Line Explanation

#!/bin/bash

This is called a shebang. It tells the operating system: “Run this file using the bash shell.”
Without this line, the system might not know how to run the script.

echo

The echo command prints messages to the terminal. It’s a simple way to give feedback while the script runs:
echo "Creating environment..."
You’ll often use this to keep the user informed of progress.

conda create -y -n orbitviz python=3.10

Let’s break this down:
conda is a package and environment manager, especially useful for scientific work.
create tells it to make a new environment.
-n orbitviz gives the environment a name.
python=3.10 installs Python 3.10 in that environment.
-y means “yes to all prompts” — it won’t ask for confirmation.
Why use environments?
They keep your projects isolated. This way, a change in one project (e.g. upgrading NumPy) won’t break another.

conda activate orbitviz || source activate orbitviz This tries to activate the environment so all future commands run inside it.

conda activate orbitviz: Standard command for modern conda setups.
|| source activate orbitviz: This part runs only if the first one fails (older conda versions).

conda install -n orbitviz -c conda-forge astropy=5.3 This installs a package called astropy from the conda-forge channel:

-n orbitviz: Install into this environment.
-c conda-forge: Use the conda-forge channel — a community-driven source of scientific packages.
astropy=5.3: Install exactly version 5.3.
Why a specific version? Not all versions of Astropy work well with Poliastro. Version pinning helps avoid compatibility issues.
This logic repeats for:
matplotlib=3.5
jupyterlab
plotly
numpy, scipy, and tqdm.

conda run -n orbitviz pip install poliastro[all]

Sometimes, we need pip to install packages from PyPI (Python Package Index).

conda run -n orbitviz: Run a command inside the environment.
pip install poliastro[all]: Install Poliastro and all its optional features.


chmod +x setup_orbitviz.sh

Before you run the script, you make it executable with:
chmod +x setup_orbitviz.sh
chmod changes file permissions.
+x means “make this file executable.”
Now you can run it as:
./setup_orbitviz.sh

title: Automating a Scientific Python Setup: A Gentle Walkthrough
text:
Why Do Versions Matter?
Scientific libraries like astropy, matplotlib, and poliastro evolve constantly. But newer isn’t always better—especially when libraries depend on each other.
For example:

Poliastro might rely on internal behavior of Astropy 5.3 that’s changed in 5.4.
Matplotlib might break visualization formatting if you jump versions.

Version pinning ensures a stable and predictable environment—which is critical when you’re doing simulations or research.

title: Automating a Scientific Python Setup: A Gentle Walkthrough
text:
Want to try?
Here’s how you can run the whole thing:
# Make the script executable
chmod +x setup_orbitviz.sh

# Run it!
./setup_orbitviz.sh
If something fails (e.g. activation), try this manually:
conda activate orbitviz
And then:
jupyterlab

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
text:
This post continues my series on poliastro, a modern Python library for orbital mechanics.
If you’re new to poliastro, you may want to read these first:
In this article, I’ll dissect a compact program that plots an orbit and marks the spacecraft’s current position. The focus is on what each line does and why it’s written that way.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
text:
The Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from astropy import units as u
from poliastro.bodies import Earth
from poliastro.twobody import Orbit
from poliastro.plotting.static import StaticOrbitPlotter

def plot_and_save(orbit, filename, options=None):
    if options is None:
        options = {}

    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    plotter = StaticOrbitPlotter(ax)
    plotter.plot(orbit)

    # Marker at current position
    marker_color = options.get("marker_color", "ro")
    ax.plot(*orbit.r.to(u.km).value[:2], marker_color)

    # Title and styling
    ax.set_title(options.get("title", "Orbit Plot"))
    if not options.get("show_legend", False):
        ax.legend().remove()
    if not options.get("show_grid", False):
        ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_facecolor(options.get("background", "white"))

    fig.savefig(filename, dpi=options.get("dpi", 300), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
section: Imports: What we’re bringing in (and why)
text:
Imports: What we’re bringing in (and why)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Matplotlib is the plotting workhorse. We use it to create the figure/axes and to save the image.

from astropy import units as u

units comes from Astropy and is central to scientific correctness.
Any physical value (like position, velocity) can be a Quantity: a number
with units attached (e.g., kilometers, meters per second).
Using Quantity lets the library enforce unit consistency and convert units safely.

from poliastro.bodies import Earth
from poliastro.twobody import Orbit
from poliastro.plotting.static import StaticOrbitPlotter

Earth is a predefined body with constants you’d expect (e.g., μ).
Orbit is the class that represents an orbit, either from classical elements or from a state vector.
StaticOrbitPlotter handles drawing the orbit on a Matplotlib axes (2D static view).

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
section: Function signature and the “mutable default” pattern

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
section: Creating the figure and the orbit plotter
text:
Creating the figure and the orbit plotter
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plotter = StaticOrbitPlotter(ax)
plotter.plot(orbit)

plt.subplots() returns a Figure (the overall canvas) and an Axes (a plotting region). You can have multiple axes on a single figure; think “subplots on one canvas”.
StaticOrbitPlotter(ax) binds the plotter to our axes.
plotter.plot(orbit) draws the orbit curve on the axes (the trajectory).

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
text:
Marking the current position
marker_color = options.get("marker_color", "ro")
ax.plot(*orbit.r.to(u.km).value[:2], marker_color)
options.get("marker_color", "ro")

.get(key, default) looks up a key in a dict and returns the value if present, otherwise the provided default.
Here, if the user doesn’t pass a marker_color option, we default to ro (Matplotlib shorthand for red o-marker).


What is orbit.r?

orbit.r is an instance of Quantity class defined in Astropy — specifically, a 3-component position vector with units (e.g., [x, y, z] in kilometers or meters).
Being a Quantity means unit conversions and consistency checks are handled for you.

.to(u.km)

Converts the Quantity to kilometers.
If the vector is already in km, it’s effectively a no-op; if not, it’s converted safely.

.value

On an astropy.units.Quantity, .value removes the units and returns a plain NumPy array. Here, after .to(u.km), you get something like array([x_km, y_km, z_km]).

[:2]

We’re drawing a 2D projection (x–y plane). [:2] slices the first two components (x and y), ignoring z.

* (argument unpacking)

ax.plot wants x, y as two separate arguments.
We currently have an array of two numbers. The * operator unpacks that array, so the call becomes ax.plot(x, y, marker_color) rather than ax.plot([x, y], marker_color).

Result: a marker is placed at the satellite’s current position on the plotted trajectory.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
text:
Title and styling
ax.set_title(options.get("title", "Orbit Plot"))

if not options.get("show_legend", False):
    ax.legend().remove()

if not options.get("show_grid", False):
    ax.grid(False)

ax.set_facecolor(options.get("background", "white"))
options.get("show_legend", False)

Looks up show_legend in options.
If missing, it defaults to False.


Understanding if not … precisely

The if statement expects a Boolean.
not flips it: not True → False, not False → True.

Let’s enumerate the cases for the legend:


Case 1: show_legend = True

options.get("show_legend", False) → True
if not True → if False → block is skipped
No removal → the legend stays.



Case 2: show_legend = False

options.get("show_legend", False) → False
if not False → if True → block runs
ax.legend().remove() → the legend is removed.



Case 3: show_legend missing

options.get("show_legend", False) → default False
Same as Case 2 → legend is removed.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
section: Saving the figure and cleaning up
text:
Saving the figure and cleaning up
fig.savefig(filename, dpi=options.get("dpi", 300), bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

dpi: output resolution. 300 is a good default for documents.
bbox_inches="tight": trims extra whitespace around the figure.
plt.close(fig): frees memory (important if you batch-generate many plots).

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro — A Detailed Walkthrough
text:
Minimal working examples
from astropy import units as u
from poliastro.bodies import Earth
from poliastro.twobody import Orbit
from astropy.time import Time

# Example: circular-ish LEO from classical elements
epoch = Time("2025-08-01 00:00:00", scale="utc")
a = (Earth.R.to(u.km) + 500 * u.km)             # semi-major axis: Earth radius + 500 km
ecc = 0.001 * u.one
inc = 51.6 * u.deg
raan = 40.0 * u.deg
argp = 0.0 * u.deg
nu = 0.0 * u.deg

leo = Orbit.from_classical(Earth, a, ecc, inc, raan, argp, nu, epoch=epoch)

options = {
    "title": "LEO ~500 km (x–y projection)",
    "marker_color": "bo",       # blue circle
    "show_legend": False,
    "show_grid": True,
    "background": "white",
    "dpi": 300
}

plot_and_save(leo, "leo_xy.png", options)
If you instead have a state vector (r, v) at an epoch:
r = [7000, 0, 0] * u.km
v = [0, 7.5, 1] * (u.km / u.s)
state_orbit = Orbit.from_vectors(Earth, r, v, epoch=epoch)
plot_and_save(state_orbit, "state_xy.png", options)

Poliastro is a fantastic tool for visualizing satellite orbits. In this post, we not only plotted orbits but also found opportunities to work with Python dictionaries and touch on a few other programming concepts along the way.

title: How AI will Redfine Human Roles in Space Software
text: Artificial Intelligence is reshaping software development at a breathtaking pace. What used to take teams of engineers months or years can now be prototyped in hours with the help of tools like ChatGPT. The shift is not simply about speed — it’s about cost. The marginal cost of producing code has collapsed, and that has profound implications for engineers in every industry, especially space.

title: How AI will Redfine Human Roles in Space Software
section: Technology has always made things cheaper
text:
Technology has always made things cheaper
Every wave of technology has reduced the cost of something. Consider Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI), which pushed the cost of a single semiconductor gate effectively to zero. That breakthrough allowed engineers to pack millions of gates into a single chip, enabling the rise of personal computers, smartphones, and ultimately the AI systems we use today.
Without VLSI, AI would still be an elite tool for the few. With it, the most advanced technology in human history is literally available to anyone with a smartphone and an internet connection.
AI is playing a similar role for software. What used to be scarce — high-quality code — is rapidly becoming abundant.

title: How AI will Redfine Human Roles in Space Software
section: How AI is reshaping software development
text:
How AI is reshaping software development
Traditionally, writing software meant long hours of typing, debugging, and maintaining code. AI flips this model. The human’s role is no longer “code producer” but “problem architect.”

The human defines the structure of the program.
The human decides what needs to be tested and how.
The AI generates the implementation, while the human stays active and vigilant — reviewing, refining, and stress-testing what comes out.

It’s not about outsourcing thinking. It’s about elevating the human role to where it matters most.

title: How AI will Redfine Human Roles in Space Software
text:
Domain knowledge becomes the premium
When the effort of writing code drops to near zero, what becomes valuable is not syntax knowledge but domain expertise. The premium is on people who deeply understand the system they are working with, and who can translate that knowledge into precise prompts, rigorous test plans, and meaningful reviews.
This is where scientists, engineers, and researchers stand to benefit enormously. Many of them already possess deep expertise in their domains but have not always had the time or training to produce robust, reusable software. With AI, modest knowledge of software best practices — combined with their expertise — is enough to produce high-quality tools usable by broader teams.
For professional software developers, the bar shifts. It is no longer enough to know how to code. They must:

Strengthen their domain knowledge.
Learn to articulate problems as strong prompts.
Master the art of reviewing AI-generated code.
Design tests that reflect real-world conditions, not just “happy paths.”

In short: coding itself is no longer the scarce skill. Thinking deeply about the problem is.

title: How AI will Redfine Human Roles in Space Software
text:
The space industry example
Few fields illustrate this better than space. Satellites are systems of systems: power, thermal, communications, payload, and attitude control are all intertwined.
Traditionally, a young engineer might enter the field specializing in one subsystem, such as Attitude Determination and Control (ADCS). They would be aware that their work interacts with power or thermal, but their focus would remain on ADCS alone. Only with years of experience would they begin to see the satellite as a whole system.
AI changes this expectation. With the heavy lifting of coding handled, engineers will increasingly be expected to explore coupled effects earlier in their careers. Instead of just calculating pointing accuracy, they might simulate how attitude affects solar power generation and thermal loads — and do so in a single integrated workflow.
In other words, AI forces us to stop treating a satellite as a collection of silos. It pushes us to see it as one unified system.

title: How AI will Redfine Human Roles in Space Software
text:
Conclusion
The cost of code has collapsed, but the value of human expertise has never been higher. In the AI era, the “default engineer” in space will not be someone confined to one subsystem, but someone capable of thinking across the entire satellite.
The winners will be those who pair deep domain knowledge with a collaborative approach to AI — writing strong prompts, reviewing critically, and testing rigorously.
This is not the end of engineering. It’s the beginning of a new kind of engineer.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro – Part 1: Creating Orbit Objects
text:
Poliastro is a modern Python library for orbital mechanics. It’s designed for both educational use and practical analysis, and integrates beautifully with Python tools like Astropy and Matplotlib.
In this post, we’ll learn how to define orbits in Poliastro using both state vectors and orbital elements. We won’t dive into plotting yet — we’ll just set up the orbits. Visualizations will come in a follow-up article.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro – Part 1: Creating Orbit Objects
text:
Poliastro is a modern Python library for orbital mechanics. It’s designed for both educational use and practical analysis, and integrates beautifully with Python tools like Astropy and Matplotlib.
In this post, we’ll learn how to define orbits in Poliastro using both state vectors and orbital elements. We won’t dive into plotting yet — we’ll just set up the orbits. Visualizations will come in a follow-up article.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro – Part 1: Creating Orbit Objects
text:
Understanding the imports
from poliastro.bodies import Earth
from poliastro.twobody import Orbit
from poliastro.plotting.static import StaticOrbitPlotter
from astropy import units as u
from astropy.time import Time
Let’s break these down:

Earth is a predefined object representing Earth, with built-in values
for radius, mass, and gravitational constant.
Orbit is the main class for representing orbits using either position/velocity vectors or classical elements.
StaticOrbitPlotter will let us visualize the orbit using Matplotlib (we won’t use it in this post).
units comes from Astropy — it allows us to specify and enforce physical units in our calculations.
Time is used to represent specific epochs (times) for orbital calculations.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro – Part 1: Creating Orbit Objects
text:
The Earth Object in Poliastro
When you run from poliastro.bodies import Earth, you’re import a predefined instance of the SolarSystemPlanet class. It comes with physical constants like:
Earth.R       # Radius of Earth
Earth.k       # Gravitational parameter (GM)
Earth.mass    # Mass
These are essential when calculating orbits.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro – Part 1: Creating Orbit Objects
text:
Creating Orbit Objects
There are two ways to create an orbit in Poliastro:

Using Position and Velocity Vectors

r = [7000, 0, 0] * u.km
v = [0, 7.5, 1] * u.km / u.s
epoch = Time("2025-01-01", scale="utc")

orbit1 = Orbit.from_vectors(Earth, r, v, epoch=epoch)
This method is useful when you have raw observational data or simulation outputs.
Note: When creating orbits from vectors, epoch is required. This is the time at which the vectors are valid.

Using Classical Orbital Elements

You can also define an orbit using elements like:

Semi-major axis (a): average size of the orbit
Eccentricity (ecc): shape of the orbit
Inclination (inc): tilt of the orbit relative to Earth’s equator
RAAN: Right Ascension of the Ascending Node
Argument of perigee (argp)
True anomaly (nu): position of the object along the orbit

Here’s how to define a circular orbit at 500 km altitude with a 30° inclination:
a_circ = Earth.R + 500 * u.km
inc_circ = 30 * u.deg
orbit2 = Orbit.circular(Earth, alt=500 * u.km, inc=inc_circ)
Now, let’s define an elliptical orbit with perigee at 500 km and apogee at 1500 km:
r_p = Earth.R + 500 * u.km  # Perigee
r_a = Earth.R + 1500 * u.km # Apogee

a = (r_p + r_a) / 2                     # Semi-major axis
ecc = (r_a - r_p) / (r_a + r_p)        # Eccentricity
inc = 60 * u.deg                       # Inclination
raan = 30 * u.deg
argp = 0 * u.deg
nu = 0 * u.deg

orbit3 = Orbit.from_classical(Earth, a, ecc, inc, raan, argp, nu)
Note: You don’t need to provide epoch when creating orbits using classical elements — the default is J2000, the standard astronomical epoch corresponding to January 1, 2000, 12:00 TT.

A Note on Units and u.one
Poliastro uses Astropy Units to manage dimensions. That’s why you’ll often see values like:
ecc = 0.1 * u.one  # Eccentricity is dimensionless
Here, u.one is a special unit that denotes “dimensionless” quantities. This ensures compatibility with Astropy’s quantity system while preserving physical correctness.


What is J2000?
J2000 refers to January 1, 2000, 12:00 TT (Terrestrial Time). It’s a standard epoch used in astronomy and orbital mechanics.
In Poliastro, if you don’t specify an epoch, it defaults to J2000. Since Poliastro assumes perfect Keplerian motion (i.e., no perturbations), these orbits don’t change over time — so using J2000 as the default epoch is a safe baseline.

title: Visualizing Orbits with Poliastro – Part 1: Creating Orbit Objects
text:
Summary
In this post, we learnt how to:

Import and use Poliastro’s core modules
Define orbits using state vectors or classical elements
Handle physical units properly using Astropy
Understand default behavior like epoch and dimensionless quantities
In the next post, we’ll use StaticOrbitPlotter to visualize these orbits with Matplotlib.

This is part of an ongoing experiment in human–AI collaboration for technical learning and writing.

title: What the Radius–Velocity Angle Reveals About Orbit Direction
text:
We want a clear, intuitive answer to: given the true anomaly \(\theta\), how can we tell from the geometry whether a satellite in an elliptical orbit is moving toward perigee or away from it?
We will first give a short, intuitive argument (no heavy algebra), then derive an explicit formula for the angle \(\psi\) between the position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) and velocity vector \(\mathbf{v}\).

title: What the Radius–Velocity Angle Reveals About Orbit Direction
text:
We want a clear, intuitive answer to: given the true anomaly \(\theta\), how can we tell from the geometry whether a satellite in an elliptical orbit is moving toward perigee or away from it?
We will first give a short, intuitive argument (no heavy algebra), then derive an explicit formula for the angle \(\psi\) between the position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) and velocity vector \(\mathbf{v}\).

title: What the Radius–Velocity Angle Reveals About Orbit Direction
section: Quick, intuitive argument (sign of radial velocity)
text:
Quick, intuitive argument (sign of radial velocity)
Decompose the velocity into radial and transverse components: \[
\mathbf{v} = v_r\,\hat{\mathbf r} + v_\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}.
\tag{1}\]
The cosine of the angle \(\psi\) between \(\mathbf r\) and \(\mathbf v\) is \[
\cos\psi = \frac{\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v}{r\,v} = \frac{r v_r}{r v} = \frac{v_r}{v},
\tag{2}\] so the sign of \(v_r\) alone determines whether \(\psi\) is less than or greater than \(90^\circ\).
The radial component of velocity is simply \(\dot{r}\) — the time rate of change of the satellite’s distance from Earth.

When the satellite moves away from perigee (the closest point), its distance from Earth is growing until it reaches a maximum at apogee. In this phase, \(\dot{r} > 0\), so the radial velocity \(v_r\) is positive.
When the satellite moves back toward perigee, its distance is shrinking until it reaches a minimum again at perigee. Here, \(\dot{r} < 0\), so \(v_r\) is negative.

We can now conclude:

If \(v_r > 0\), then \(\cos \psi > 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \psi < 90^\circ\). In this case, the velocity has a growing radial component, meaning the satellite is moving away from perigee toward apogee.
If \(v_r < 0\), then \(\cos \psi < 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \psi > 90^\circ\). Here, the velocity has a shrinking radial component, meaning the satellite is moving back toward perigee from apogee.

Thus, a quick test for “toward/away” is simply the sign of \(v_r\).

title: What the Radius–Velocity Angle Reveals About Orbit Direction
section: Full derivation: express \(\cos\psi\) in terms of \(e\) and \(\theta\)
text:
Full derivation: express \(\cos\psi\) in terms of \(e\) and \(\theta\)
Below we derive an explicit relation \(\cos\psi=\cos\psi(\theta)\) so a reader can compute \(\psi\) (not only its sign).

Orbit geometry
The orbit in polar coordinates (focus at origin) is \[
r(\theta) = \frac{p}{1 + e\cos\theta}, \qquad p = a(1-e^2), \quad 0<e<1.
\tag{3}\]


Radial velocity via the chain rule
Because \(r=r(\theta(t))\), \[
v_r \equiv \dot r = \frac{dr}{dt} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\,\dot\theta.
\tag{4}\]
Differentiate \(r(\theta)\) with respect to \(\theta\): \[
\frac{dr}{d\theta}
= \frac{d}{d\theta}\!\left(\frac{p}{1+e\cos\theta}\right)
= \frac{p\,e\sin\theta}{(1+e\cos\theta)^2}.
\tag{5}\]
Specific angular momentum gives \[
h = r^2\dot\theta = \sqrt{\mu p},
\tag{6}\] so \(\dot\theta = h/r^2\). Using \(r=\dfrac{p}{1+e\cos\theta}\) and substituting into Equation 4: \[
\begin{aligned}
v_r
&= \frac{p\,e\sin\theta}{(1+e\cos\theta)^2}\cdot\frac{h}{r^2} \\
&= \frac{p\,e\sin\theta}{(1+e\cos\theta)^2}\cdot\frac{h(1+e\cos\theta)^2}{p^2} \\
&= \frac{h}{p}\,e\sin\theta
= \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{p}}\,e\sin\theta.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]


Transverse component and speed
From \(h = r v_\theta\), \[
v_\theta = \frac{h}{r} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{p}}\,(1+e\cos\theta).
\tag{8}\]
Then the speed is \[
\begin{aligned}
v &= \sqrt{v_r^2 + v_\theta^2} \\
&= \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{p}\Big(e^2\sin^2\theta + (1+e\cos\theta)^2\Big)} \\
&= \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{p}}\sqrt{1 + 2e\cos\theta + e^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}\]


Final formula for \(\cos\psi\)
Using Equation 2, Equation 7 and Equation 9 we get \[
\boxed{%
\cos\psi(\theta) = \frac{e\sin\theta}{\sqrt{\,1 + 2e\cos\theta + e^2\,}}%
}
\tag{10}\]

title: What the Radius–Velocity Angle Reveals About Orbit Direction
section: Why the denominator is always positive (ellipses)
text:
Why the denominator is always positive (ellipses)
The term under the square root can be rearranged as \[
1 + 2e\cos\theta + e^2 = (1+e\cos\theta)^2 + e^2\sin^2\theta,
\tag{11}\] which is a sum of two non-negative terms. For \(0<e<1\) there is no \(\theta\) making both terms zero simultaneously (that would require \(\cos\theta=-1/e\), impossible). Hence the denominator in Equation 10 is strictly positive for elliptic orbits.
As a simple check, at \(\theta=\pi\) the expression becomes \((1-e)^2>0\).

title: What the Radius–Velocity Angle Reveals About Orbit Direction
text:
Conclusion
We can now conclude the following.
Since the velocity vector in an elliptical orbit always has a tangential component, the angle \(\psi\) between \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) is restricted to the physically meaningful range
\[
0^\circ < \psi < 180^\circ.
\]
The endpoints are excluded, because \(\psi = 0^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\) would imply purely radial motion, which is impossible in a bound Keplerian orbit.
Within this range:

If \(v_r > 0\), then \(\cos\psi > 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \psi < 90^\circ\) (velocity has a growing radial component → satellite moving away from perigee).
If \(v_r < 0\), then \(\cos\psi < 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \psi > 90^\circ\) (velocity has a shrinking radial component → satellite moving toward perigee).

We can express this in terms of dot product of the radius and velocity vectors:
\[
\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v} = r v \cos \psi
\]
Since \(r>0\) and \(v>0\), the sign of \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) is determined entirely by \(\cos\psi\):

If \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v} > 0\), then \(0^\circ < \psi < 90^\circ\) (satellite is moving away from perigee).
If \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v} < 0\), then \(90^\circ < \psi < 180^\circ\) (satellite is moving toward perigee).


AI Attribution: Textbooks often state that the dot product of the radius and velocity vectors indicates the direction of a satellite’s motion, but they rarely explain the reasoning in detail. I explored this idea in depth through a long conversation with AI, making detailed notes along the way. The first draft of this post grew out of those notes, and I refined it further with AI’s help.
